concepts.title: Vectors
concepts.question: What is a vector, and which two operations make a set of them a vector space?
concepts.answer:
A vector is an element of a vector space: an object that can be added to other vectors and scaled by numbers. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ it is an ordered list $v=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$.

The two operations are

- addition: $u+v=(u_1+v_1,\dots,u_n+v_n)$
- scalar multiplication: $\lambda v=(\lambda v_1,\dots,\lambda v_n)$

They must satisfy the usual axioms (associativity, commutativity, zero vector, additive inverses, distributivity).

concepts.title: Linear combination
concepts.question: What is a linear combination of vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$?
concepts.answer:
Any vector of the form

$$\lambda_1 v_1+\lambda_2 v_2+\dots+\lambda_k v_k,\qquad \lambda_i\in\mathbb{R}.$$

Example: $(5,4)=5\,(1,0)+4\,(0,1)$ is a linear combination of $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$.

concepts.title: Span
concepts.question: What is the span of a set of vectors, and why is it a subspace?
concepts.answer:
$\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_k)$ is the set of all linear combinations of $v_1,\dots,v_k$.

It is a subspace: it contains $0$ (all coefficients zero), and a sum or scalar multiple of linear combinations is again a linear combination.

The span is the smallest subspace containing the vectors.

concepts.title: Linear independence
concepts.question: When are vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ linearly independent?
concepts.answer:
When the only solution of

$$\lambda_1 v_1+\dots+\lambda_k v_k=0$$

is $\lambda_1=\dots=\lambda_k=0$.

Equivalently, no $v_i$ is a linear combination of the others. Example: $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are independent; $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ are not, since $2\,(1,2)-(2,4)=0$.

concepts.title: Basis
concepts.question: What is a basis of a vector space?
concepts.answer:
A list of vectors that is linearly independent **and** spans the space.

Every vector $v$ then has a *unique* expression $v=\lambda_1 b_1+\dots+\lambda_n b_n$; the $\lambda_i$ are its coordinates.

Example: $(1,0),(0,1)$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

concepts.title: Dimension
concepts.question: How is the dimension of a vector space defined, and why is it well defined?
concepts.answer:
$\dim V$ is the number of vectors in any basis of $V$.

It is well defined because all bases of $V$ have the same size (a consequence of the Steinitz exchange lemma: an independent list is never longer than a spanning list).

Example: $\dim\mathbb{R}^n=n$.

concepts.title: Matrix
concepts.question: What is a matrix, and how does it act on a vector?
concepts.answer:
An $m\times n$ matrix $A$ is a rectangular array of numbers. It defines a linear map $\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, $x\mapsto Ax$, where

$$(Ax)_i=\sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}x_j.$$

Equivalently, $Ax$ is the linear combination of the columns of $A$ with coefficients $x_1,\dots,x_n$.

concepts.title: Rank
concepts.question: What is the rank of a matrix and how do you compute it?
concepts.answer:
$\operatorname{rank}(A)$ is the dimension of the column space (the span of the columns) of $A$; it equals the dimension of the row space.

Compute it by Gaussian elimination: the rank is the number of pivots.

Rank-nullity: for $A$ with $n$ columns, $\operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim\ker A=n$.
